newsitem.title: UK: Regulation - How countries police financial markets.
newsitem.headline: Regulation - How countries police financial markets.

text.p: British Chancellor of the Exchequer Gordon Brown stunned the City on Tuesday with a proposal to bring regulation of the financial industry under one umbrella.
The move sets Britain apart from many of the world's other major economies where regulation is often carved up according to various sectors such as banking, securites and insurance.
A summary of how other countries handle regulation follows:
BRITAIN
- Proposals announced on Tuesday by Brown would make the Securities Investments Board (SIB) the sole regulator of the financial industry in Britain.

- The SIB will take up responsibility from self-regulating organisations set up under the Conservative government in 1996. It will also take up responsibility for banking supervision, previously the role of the Bank of England.
GERMANY
- Regulation here is split between four authorities:
1) the Bundesaufsichtsamt fuer das Kreditwesen -- which regulates banks;
2) the Bundesaufsichtsamt fuer Wertpapiere -- which regulates financial markets;
3) the Bundsaufsichtsamt fuer Versicherung - which regulates insurers, and;
4)the Bundesbank, which has a watchdog function in overseeing credit relations between financial houses and can call on one of the other bodies to intervene if necessary.
- The Bundesbank however does not have the kind of regulatory power that the Bank of England previously had but does play a standback role in overseeing regulation.
UNITED STATES
- The Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) is the official U.S. body responsible for regulatory oversight and administering rules associated with the securities.
- The Commodities Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulates most exchange-traded derivatives
- The Federal Reserve and Office of the Comptroller of the Currency and state bank regulators regulate bank activity -Insurance is regulated at the state level.
- Debate about financial regulation in the United States has reached fever pitch in recent months.
President Bill Clinton's admistration will soon unveil plans to update U.S. banking laws, including those covering
regulation.
The reforms are likely to tear down some of the Depression-era barriers separating banking from securities and insurance.

Also, many of the big U.S. exchanges -- arguing excessive regulation is driving business abroad and to the blooming over-the-counter market -- are backing a proposed bill that would create a "professional market" for trading on some exchanges which would allow more flexible rules.
FRANCE
-The Comite de la Reglementation Bancaire (CRB), chaired by the Finance Minister with the governor of the French central bank as vice-chairman, regulates banking.

-The Commission Bancaire, which is headed by the governor of the Bank of France and includes the director of the Treasury and four members appointed by the ministry, is responsible for implementing the rules laid down by the CRB.

-The Conseil des Marches Financiers has responsibility for the functioning of both the stock and bond markets -The Commission des Operations de Bourse is a watchdog body with responsibility for savings, portfolio management companies and financial information provided to the markets.
-COB members are nominated by the upper and lower houses of parliament and an economic and social council.
JAPAN

-Japan's "Big Bang" reform plans aim to liberalise financial markets by 2001 by ending fixed commissions for stock brokers, increasing the release of financial information and allow banks, securities houses and insurance companies to endter each others now protected areas.
- Both the Ministry of Finance and Bank of Japan are responsible for industry regulation.
